title: Adab of the market
hookLine: a hand pushed into a heap of grain comes out wet

lines: WHY NOT PUT IT ON TOP?
cards: The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, is walking through the market, past a seller's heap of grain. He pushes his hand into it, deep, and his fingers come out wet. It's in Sahih Muslim.
He asks the seller what this is. Rain got to it, the seller says. And the Prophet answers, in paraphrase: then why didn't you put the wet part on top, so people could see it?
Then one short sentence about anyone who cheats, and it's the hardest line in today's lesson.

teach.h: WHOEVER CHEATS IS NOT OF ME.
teach.b: The sentence is: whoever cheats is not of me. Notice what the seller had done. He hadn't soaked the grain himself; rain did that.
His fault was letting the dry grain hide the wet. In this adab, honesty has to be visible. The Qur'an says the same in the language of scales.

Al-Mutaffifin, the defrauders, opens like this, in Pickthall's translation: "Woe unto the defrauders: Those who when they take the measure from mankind demand it full, But if they measure unto them or weigh for them, they cause them loss."
Full measure when buying, short measure when selling: the verse catches the double standard.

Then hoarding. A hadith in Sahih Muslim says, in paraphrase, that no one hoards except a sinner: buying up what people need and holding it back until they're desperate. The market is meant to feed people, not corner them.
And the line this day is named for.

In Sahih al-Bukhari, in paraphrase: may Allah have mercy on a man who is easygoing when he sells, easygoing when he buys, and easygoing when he asks for what he's owed. The last, collecting a debt, is easy to skip.
Another hadith in Bukhari: if buyer and seller are truthful and make things clear, their deal is blessed; if they hide things and lie, the blessing is wiped away.
Honesty you can see, no profiting from need, and ease on both sides of the counter.

how: Muslims are taught to trade by full measure, disclose a product's faults, avoid hoarding, and be easygoing when buying, selling and collecting debts, citing al-Mutaffifin and the hadith of the heap of grain.

games.q: what does “adab of the market” mean?
o: getting the best possible price every time
honest scales and ease in buying and selling
never selling anything that has a small flaw

games.q: the adab of the market — tap the pairs.
p: no one does it but a sinner

s: the seller had soaked the grain himself
rain did it; his fault was hiding the wet grain under the dry.
truthfulness brings blessing to a deal
Bukhari: if buyer and seller are truthful and make things clear, their deal is blessed.
the hadith asks for ease only from the seller
easygoing when he sells, when he buys, and when he asks for what he's owed.

games.q: rain soaked the bottom of your grain. the top is dry and looks perfect. what do you do?
o: leave the dry grain on top.
put the wet grain on top, where buyers can see it.
games.why: the Prophet asked the seller why he hadn't put the wet part on top so people could see it: whoever cheats is not of me.

practice: Bring to mind one exchange coming up, a purchase, a bill, a refund, something you're selling, someone who owes you, and notice where you'd usually press hard, or grumble, or let the wet grain stay hidden.

Now see it done the hadith's way: a fair price said plainly, any flaw said out loud, and a little more patience than you'd planned for whoever owes you. If you pray, you can ask for barakah, blessing, in your dealings.

wordCard.voice: Adab of the market. The manners of buying and selling: honest scales, nothing hidden, no hoarding, and ease when you sell, buy, and ask for what you're owed. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: easygoing, generous in dealing; the hadith's word for the buyer and seller.

carryVoice: Your line: easy in dealing. Honesty you can see. That's one thousand three hundred days.
